disputes: Two translations: the entries had followed Robert Brinkley's translation of ch. 3 (Mississippi Review, 1983) while citing Dana Polan's (1986). Where the wording differs ('makes'/'constructs', 'strong'/'high coefficient'), the entries now quote Polan, the translation cited and read. 'Exuberance' came from De Balsi's account of the passage; Polan has 'exhilaration' (p. 19).

Minor and small: De Balsi notes that Kafka's own diary word is 'small' and that 'mineure' comes from Marthe Robert's French translation of the diaries. The book draws on Kafka's diary entry of 25 December 1911 (pp. 17–19, notes 2, 3 and 6), and its notes quote that entry in English as 'a small nation's memory' (p. 93), without discussing the word. Kafka's diaries were not read; De Balsi's note is kept as hers, and the book's quotation is consistent with it.

new_d.text: In Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature (1975), the literature a minority builds inside a major language, marked by the deterritorialization of language, the immediate political charge of every individual matter and a collective value.

new_text.text: Deleuze and Guattari call a minor literature “that which a minority constructs within a major language” (p. 16), and their case is Franz Kafka, a Jew of Prague writing in German, who in their reading names the impasse facing the Jews of Prague: they cannot help writing, cannot write in German, and cannot write in another language (p. 16).
Pages of Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature are from Dana Polan's translation (1986).

They give it three characteristics (pp. 16–18): its language is affected with a “high coefficient of deterritorialization” (p. 16); everything in it is political, since its “cramped space” connects each individual concern immediately to politics (p. 17); and everything in it takes on a collective value, so that literature becomes the people's concern (pp. 17–18).
The word minor, they conclude, names “the revolutionary conditions for every literature” inside an established one (p. 18).
Kafka's own word, Sara De Balsi notes, is small (petites littératures in French), and the adjective mineure comes from Marthe Robert's 1954 translation of his diaries.

The authors see two ways of pushing a deterritorialized language further (p. 19): the symbolic reterritorialization of the Prague school, Gustav Meyrink and Max Brod among them, whose politics ends in Zionism and the “dream of Zion”, and Kafka's way, which takes the German of Prague as it is, “in its very poverty”, toward sobriety (p. 19).
They ask whether Joyce and Beckett show the same two paths: Joyce operating “by exhilaration and overdetermination”, Beckett by “dryness and sobriety, a willed poverty” (p. 19).

Kafka's aim, they write, is a minor use of his own language, to be “a sort of stranger within his own language” (p. 26), and near its end the chapter calls on writing to “create a becoming-minor” (p. 27).
De Balsi holds that only some writers in a second language make a minor literature, and treats it as one possible path for translingual writing.
A Thousand Plateaus returns to the minor in its fourth plateau.

Minor languages exist only in relation to a major language, which they invest in order to make it minor (p. 105), and the authors characterize them here by “a sobriety and variation”, a becoming-minor of the major language (p. 104).

The same page counts the German of Prague among minor languages and reads its alleged poverty as “a restriction of constants” and its overload as “an extension of variations” (p. 104), and minor authors, Deleuze and Guattari write, are foreigners in their own tongue (p. 105).

Majority implies a constant serving as a standard measure, and the minority is “the becoming of everybody” (p. 105); continuous variation, they write, constitutes the becoming-minoritarian of everybody (p. 106).
The same plateau sets minor sciences against the royal or major science of Euclid's invariants (p. 109), and the twelfth plateau speaks of a nomad or minor science (p. 361).
Pages of A Thousand Plateaus are from Brian Massumi's translation (1987).

rhizome.old: Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature (1975) already calls Kafka's work a rhizome, a burrow with many entrances, none of them privileged, and A Thousand Plateaus calls the burrow an animal rhizome with multiple entryways (p. 12).
rhizome.new: Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature (1975) opens by calling Kafka's work “a rhizome, a burrow”, with multiple entrances, none more privileged than another (p. 3); A Thousand Plateaus calls the burrow an animal rhizome with multiple entryways (p. 12).
rhizome.note: The book's second sentence (p. 3); quotation 'a rhizome, a burrow' checked.
rhizome.fix: quoted and paged; Polan page note added

deterritorialization.old: Language can be deterritorialized too: in Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature (1975) the German of Prague's Jewish writers has a strong coefficient of deterritorialization.
deterritorialization.new: Language can be deterritorialized too: in Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature (1975) the language of a minor literature is affected with a “high coefficient of deterritorialization” (p. 16), and the German of Prague is a deterritorialized language (p. 17).
deterritorialization.note: The book gives the coefficient to the language of minor literature in general (p. 16) and calls Prague German deterritorialized (p. 17); 'strong' was Brinkley's word.

deterritorialization.old: Sara De Balsi sets out the two paths the authors see: a symbolic reterritorialization, which they find in Max Brod, and an absolute deterritorialization, the path of minor literature, Kafka's use of Prague German in its very poverty.
deterritorialization.new: The authors find in the Prague school a symbolic reterritorialization (p. 19), and in Kafka's sober use of Prague German an absolute deterritorialization, however slow (pp. 19, 26); Sara De Balsi sets out the same two paths.
deterritorialization.note: Credited to De Balsi; the book says both: symbolic reterritorialization on p. 19, absolute deterritorialization, 'even if it is slow', on p. 26.
deterritorialization.fix: credited to the book, De Balsi kept
